title: Comprehension
tagline: Reading an unseen passage carefully and answering questions about its meaning, word use, inference and structure.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Language (Paper 1) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus topic was taken from the official-verified ISC English registry entry; no CISCE examination paper was consulted, so every example and every practice question is original and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Comprehension questions are based on an unseen passage. The point is not to repeat the passage word for word, but to show that you have read it carefully and understood it. In the ISC English Language paper, comprehension usually asks you to respond to meaning, vocabulary in context, inference and sometimes summary or structure. The skill is reading with attention: noticing what the passage says, what it implies, and how it is put together.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Understanding literal meaning; vocabulary in context; inference; selecting evidence; summary; following the passage's structure

learningOutcomes: Read an unseen passage carefully and identify its main idea.
Locate specific information in the passage.
Work out the meaning of words and phrases from context.
Make reasonable inferences from the passage.
Summarise the passage accurately and concisely.
Support answers with reference to the text.

blocks.text: The first task in comprehension is to understand what the passage says on the surface. That means following the sequence of ideas, identifying the subject, and noticing what the writer is describing, explaining or arguing. A careful reader asks what each sentence or paragraph is doing. Sometimes a passage begins with a scene or an example before moving to a point; sometimes it states the point early and then develops it. Knowing the shape of the passage makes the questions easier.

items: Identify the topic and the main idea.
Keep track of key people, events or points.
Do not jump to conclusions before reading carefully.

items.text: If a passage opens with a description of a noisy street and then moves to the writer's opinion about noise in city life, the description is doing work: it is setting up the point that follows, not just filling space.
items.note: Understanding how a passage works is part of understanding it.

blocks.text: A common comprehension question asks for the meaning of a word or phrase as it is used in the passage. This does not always mean the dictionary definition; it means the meaning that fits that sentence. A word may have several meanings, and the right one is the one the passage is using. Useful clues include the surrounding sentence, the whole paragraph, the tone of the passage, and any contrast or explanation nearby.

items: Read the sentence containing the word carefully.
Look for clues in the surrounding sentences.
Consider whether the word has a figurative or specialised sense.
Check that the meaning fits the tone of the passage.
Do not choose the first dictionary meaning that comes to mind.

items.text: A word like 'sharp' might mean 'keen' in one passage and 'sudden' in another, depending on context. The surrounding words decide which sense is intended.

blocks.text: Inference questions ask you to work out something not stated directly. That does not mean guessing wildly; it means giving a conclusion that is supported by the passage. A good inference is guided by evidence. Another part of comprehension is understanding the writer's purpose: is the passage informing, describing, warning, persuading or reflecting? Knowing the purpose helps explain tone, word choice and emphasis.

items: Base inferences on what the passage does say.
Look for hints such as contrast, emphasis, irony or understatement.
Ask why the writer chose a particular detail or tone.
Distinguish between what is stated and what is implied.
Do not invent ideas the passage does not support.

items.text: If a passage says that a student sat staring at a blank page for half an hour and then 'wrote the first sentence slowly', the reader can infer that the student was uncertain, even though that word is not used.
items.note: Inference is a careful conclusion from evidence, not a guess.

blocks.text: Some comprehension tasks involve summary or note-making. Summary means reducing a passage to its essential points without losing accuracy or adding personal opinion. Note-making means extracting the main points quickly and clearly. Both require selecting what matters and leaving out what is merely decorative or repetitive. A good summary is shorter than the original, but still faithful to it.

items: Find the main points and leave out repetition.
Keep the summary in your own words, where appropriate.
Do not add ideas or opinions that are not in the passage.
Keep the summary proportionate to the original.
For note-making, use clear points and brief wording.

items.text: If a passage describes a school event in detail, a summary should name the event, its purpose, what happened and any important outcome, without retelling every remark.
items.note: Summary is selection, not compression by deletion alone.

keyPoints: Comprehension is about understanding, not copying.
Answer the question using the passage, not your general knowledge.
Inference should be supported by the text.
A summary must be accurate, concise and in your own words.
Notice how the passage is organised, not just what it says.
Quoting or paraphrasing carefully can strengthen an answer.
examFocus: Many marks are lost by answers that drift away from the passage or by copying large stretches of it without purpose.
For 'find the meaning' questions, stay close to the passage and choose the meaning that works there.

vocabulary.meaning: Understanding a passage and answering questions about it.
What a passage says directly, on the surface.
A conclusion drawn from evidence in the passage rather than stated outright.
The meaning of a word as used in the passage, not just its dictionary definition.
A shortened version that keeps the essential points of the original.
The writer's aim in the passage, such as to inform, describe or persuade.

questions.prompt: A comprehension answer should be based mainly on:
options: The most dramatic part of the passage
questions.explanation: Comprehension tests understanding of the given text, so answers must come from it.
questions.commonMistake: Answering from outside knowledge instead of the passage.

options: The longest dictionary definition of the word
The meaning of the word as it is used in the passage
questions.answer: The meaning of the word as it is used in the passage
questions.explanation: The meaning depends on the surrounding text, not only on the word in isolation.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the first dictionary meaning without checking the context.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a literal answer and an inferential answer? Give one example of each kind of prompt.
questions.answer: A literal answer comes from something the passage states directly, such as 'What time did the meeting begin?' An inferential answer comes from reading between the lines, such as 'What does the writer suggest about the meeting's preparation?'
questions.explanation: Literal questions ask what is said; inferential questions ask what is implied.
questions.commonMistake: Treating every question as if it were either fully factual or fully opinion-based.

questions.prompt: State two rules for writing a good summary.
questions.answer: A good summary should keep the main points, leave out unnecessary detail, and stay faithful to the passage without adding personal opinion.
questions.explanation: A summary is a compressed but accurate version of the original.
questions.commonMistake: Copying phrases from the passage or adding one's own ideas.

questions.prompt: Why is it dangerous to answer a comprehension question from memory or general knowledge instead of the passage?
questions.answer: Because the passage may include a specific detail, tone or purpose that general knowledge does not capture. A correct comprehension answer must reflect what the writer actually says or implies, not what seems likely in another situation.
questions.explanation: Comprehension rewards close reading, not outside opinion.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the passage as background and answering from one's own assumptions.
